concepts.label: The inferior salivatory nucleus provides preganglionic parasympathetic supply to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve
concepts.article_title: Inferior salivatory nucleus and the parotid gland
concepts.definition: The inferior salivatory nucleus, a general visceral efferent (parasympathetic) brainstem nucleus in the medulla, gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that travel with the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), then via its tympanic branch and the lesser petrosal nerve, to synapse in the otic ganglion; postganglionic fibres from the otic ganglion then join the auriculotemporal nerve to supply secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland. This pathway is classically contrasted with the superior salivatory nucleus, which instead supplies the submandibular, sublingual, lacrimal and nasal glands via the facial nerve. The inferior salivatory nucleus/glossopharyngeal/parotid pathway is a distinctive single-target parasympathetic route among the head's salivary glands.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve and otic ganglion.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Parasympathetic pathways of the head
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the inferior salivatory nucleus (glossopharyngeal, via the otic ganglion, supplying only the parotid) with the superior salivatory nucleus (facial nerve, supplying the submandibular, sublingual, lacrimal and nasal glands via two separate ganglia).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 2 ("inferior salivatory nucleus supplies? *parotid."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 2 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p1.

concepts.label: Benztropine, an anticholinergic, is used to treat drug-induced (extrapyramidal) tremor
concepts.definition: Benztropine is a centrally acting anticholinergic (muscarinic antagonist) that restores the normal dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia when it is disrupted by dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs (chiefly typical antipsychotics), and is used to treat the resulting drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, including tremor, rigidity and acute dystonic reactions. Its mechanism works by reducing the relative cholinergic excess that occurs when dopaminergic tone is pharmacologically blocked, rather than by directly restoring dopamine itself. This is distinct from Parkinson disease's own idiopathic dopamine-deficiency tremor, for which benztropine may also give symptomatic relief through the same cholinergic-blocking mechanism, though dopaminergic agents remain first-line there.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that benztropine, an anticholinergic, is used to treat drug-induced (extrapyramidal) tremor by rebalancing basal ganglia dopamine-acetylcholine tone.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing benztropine's anticholinergic mechanism (rebalancing dopamine-acetylcholine tone) with dopaminergic drugs (e.g. levodopa), the other, mechanistically distinct class used for tremor.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 3 ("drug x used for tremors? *benztropine."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 3 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p1.

concepts.label: Astrocytes take up glucose from cerebral capillaries via the GLUT1 glucose transporter
concepts.definition: Astrocytes, which envelop cerebral capillaries with their perivascular end-feet as part of the blood-brain barrier and the neurovascular unit, take up glucose from the capillary blood using the insulin-independent facilitative glucose transporter GLUT1, which is expressed at high density on both the capillary endothelium and the astrocyte end-foot membrane. This astrocytic glucose uptake supports the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle model, in which astrocytes metabolise glucose glycolytically to lactate and export it to neurons as an additional fuel source, particularly during high neuronal activity. GLUT1 is distinct from GLUT3, the transporter that predominates on neurons themselves for direct glucose uptake.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that astrocytes take up glucose from cerebral capillary blood via the GLUT1 transporter.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Histology > Neuroglia and blood-brain barrier
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing GLUT1 (the astrocyte/endothelial glucose transporter) with GLUT3, the transporter that predominates on neurons themselves.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 7 ("astrocyte glucose receptor? *glut1."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 7 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p1.

concepts.label: The sympathetic outflow of the spinal cord extends caudally as far as the second lumbar (L2) segment
concepts.definition: The sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow arises from preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn of the spinal cord grey matter, extending from the first thoracic (T1) segment down to the second lumbar (L2) segment, in contrast to the parasympathetic (craniosacral) outflow, which arises separately from brainstem nuclei and the sacral (S2-S4) spinal segments. L2 marks the caudal limit of this thoracolumbar sympathetic column, below which no further preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies are found in the spinal cord. This T1-L2 extent is the anatomical basis for the paravertebral sympathetic chain's own longer cranial and caudal extensions beyond the cord segments that actually contribute outflow, since ascending and descending fibres within the chain redistribute the fixed T1-L2 output to targets at other levels.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that spinal sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow extends from T1 to L2.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the thoracolumbar (T1-L2) sympathetic outflow's spinal extent with the craniosacral (brainstem plus S2-S4) parasympathetic outflow's separate origin.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 9 ("pre gangilion sympathetic? *L2."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 9 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p1. Distinct from this lane's own paper2-2018 item on the T5 sympathetic white-rami level, which was held as an unrecoverably ambiguous key rather than authored — this concept instead covers the well-supported T1-L2 overall extent of the outflow.

concepts.label: The cornea's sensory receptors are free nerve endings, making it exquisitely pain-sensitive but without specialised mechanoreceptors
concepts.definition: The cornea is densely innervated by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, but its sensory endings consist almost exclusively of bare (free) nerve endings rather than the encapsulated, specialised mechanoreceptors (e.g. Meissner's or Pacinian corpuscles) found in the skin. Because free nerve endings are predominantly nociceptors, the cornea is one of the most pain-sensitive tissues in the body, and even minor mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli are perceived chiefly as pain rather than as discriminative touch. This exclusively free-nerve-ending innervation is the physiological basis of the corneal (blink) reflex, in which even light corneal touch triggers a protective reflex blink via the trigeminal afferent and facial nerve efferent limbs.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the cornea's sensory receptors are free nerve endings, explaining its high pain sensitivity.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the cornea has specialised encapsulated mechanoreceptors like the skin, rather than recognising its receptors are exclusively free nerve endings, which is why it is predominantly pain-sensitive.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 17 ("receptors in cornea? *free nerve endings"), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 17 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p2.

concepts.label: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically in chronic alcoholics
concepts.definition: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most classically in chronic alcoholics because of a combination of poor dietary intake, impaired intestinal thiamine absorption and reduced hepatic thiamine storage capacity caused by chronic alcohol use. The acute phase, Wernicke encephalopathy, presents with the classic triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and ataxia, reflecting thiamine-dependent neuronal injury concentrated in the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey and medial thalamus; if untreated, it can progress to the chronic, often irreversible Korsakoff psychosis/amnestic syndrome, marked by severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation from mammillary body and medial thalamic damage. Because thiamine is a required cofactor for glucose metabolism, giving IV glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient without first replacing thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy, which is why thiamine is given before or with glucose in suspected cases.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency, classically in chronic alcoholics.
concepts.pitfalls: Giving IV glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient without first (or simultaneously) replacing thiamine, which can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 20 ("thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholic ? * Wernick korsakoff"), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 20 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p2.

concepts.label: The oculomotor nucleus lies in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus
concepts.article_title: Oculomotor nucleus at the superior colliculus level
concepts.definition: The oculomotor (CN III) nucleus and the adjacent Edinger-Westphal (parasympathetic) nucleus lie in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, the rostral of the two midbrain colliculi, with the emerging oculomotor nerve fibres passing ventrally through the red nucleus and out through the interpeduncular fossa. This superior-colliculus level is classically contrasted with the trochlear (CN IV) nucleus, which lies more caudally at the level of the inferior colliculus, giving the two extraocular motor cranial nerve nuclei distinct midbrain levels despite both innervating extraocular muscles. This level-based distinction is a common brainstem localisation teaching point.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the oculomotor nucleus is located in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Brainstem cranial nerve nuclei
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the oculomotor nucleus's superior-colliculus level with the trochlear nucleus's more caudal, inferior-colliculus level.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 38 ("occulomotor? *present at the level of superior colliculus."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 38 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p4.

concepts.label: The accessory olivary nuclei are not present at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation in the medulla
concepts.article_title: Accessory olivary nuclei and the level of the pyramidal decussation
concepts.definition: The medulla oblongata is cross-sectioned at several teaching levels, and the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation, the most caudal and rostral-to-the-spinal-cord level, is defined by the crossing corticospinal fibres and lacks the inferior olivary complex (the principal olivary nucleus and its accessory olivary nuclei), which only appears more rostrally, at the level of the sensory (medial lemniscus) decussation and above. This absence of the olivary nuclear complex is one of the standard identifying features used to recognise the pyramidal-decussation level on a medullary cross-section in neuroanatomy teaching, distinguishing it from the mid- and upper-medulla levels where the inferior olivary nuclear complex, including its accessory nuclei, is prominent.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the accessory olivary nuclei are absent at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation in the medulla.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the inferior olivary nuclear complex (including the accessory olivary nuclei) is present at every medullary level, rather than recognising it is absent at the low, pyramidal-decussation level and only appears more rostrally.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 42 ("not present at the level of motor decussation? *accessory olivary"), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 42 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p4.

concepts.label: Lamina I of the spinal cord grey matter (the posteromarginal nucleus) is the most posterior (dorsal-most) Rexed lamina, chiefly relaying pain and temperature
concepts.definition: In the Rexed lamination scheme of the spinal cord dorsal horn grey matter, Lamina I, also called the posteromarginal nucleus (nucleus posteromarginalis), is the thin, most dorsal (posterior-most) layer capping the dorsal horn, and it receives predominantly nociceptive (pain) and thermal (temperature) primary afferent input, chiefly from A-delta and C fibres, before relaying it onward into the ascending spinothalamic pathway. Its dorsal-most position, immediately beneath the dorsolateral tract (of Lissauer) through which these same primary afferents first enter and ascend/descend a segment or two before synapsing, is a key identifying feature distinguishing it from the deeper laminae (e.g. lamina II, the substantia gelatinosa, which modulates pain transmission via interneurons rather than directly relaying it onward).
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify lamina I (the posteromarginal nucleus) as the dorsal-most Rexed lamina, chiefly relaying pain and temperature afferents.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing lamina I (posteromarginal nucleus, dorsal-most, direct pain/temperature relay) with lamina II (substantia gelatinosa), the layer immediately deep to it that modulates rather than directly relays pain transmission.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 46 ("lamina 1? *Presents in Postmarginalis."), question-then-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, p5.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 46 of EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf (src_a7ba195b4a4d50c06da3), p5.
